en.title: Ted Lasso Season 4: Does Richmond Still Feel Like Home?
en.summary: After a three-year hiatus, the beloved Apple TV+ comedy returns, but early signs suggest it might still be grappling with the narrative bloat that plagued its previous season. Fans are eager to see if the show can recapture its magic.
en.body:
## The Lasso Effect: Back in London?

After a lengthy three-year absence, **Ted Lasso** has finally returned to our screens with its Season 4 premiere, a soft relaunch aiming to recapture the magic that made it a global phenomenon. The trailers and interviews have teased a return to London for Coach Lasso, a move that prompts immediate questions given his departure to be with his son in Kansas two years prior. The premiere, titled "Home," grapples with this very premise, attempting to justify Ted's return to the city he once called a temporary home. However, as the AV Club pointed out, the episode feels like it's spinning its wheels, dedicating a considerable 42 minutes to establishing a point that many fans likely already understood.

While the intention to explore Ted's sense of belonging in Richmond is understandable, the execution in the premiere has drawn criticism for relying on familiar, and perhaps overdone, narrative beats. The source material suggests that some characterizations, like that of Keeley Jones, have become caricaturish, and crucial plot developments are happening off-screen, leaving viewers to piece together significant shifts in the story. This pacing and reliance on exposition, rather than showing, echoes the issues that began to surface in Season 3, where overlong episodes and meandering storylines diluted the show's once-sharp focus. The lingering question is whether the showrunners have learned from these past critiques or if the familiar pitfalls remain.

## Fan Reaction and Renewal Stakes

The return of **Ted Lasso** is always met with fervent anticipation from its dedicated global fanbase, who have followed Ted's journey from optimistic American football coach to beloved soccer manager. The show's initial success was intrinsically linked to its heartwarming optimism, providing a much-needed dose of feel-good television during uncertain times. However, the criticism leveled at Season 3, particularly its pacing and narrative direction, has created a palpable sense of concern among viewers. The perceived dip in quality, culminating in what some described as a "stale cake" of a finale, has raised the stakes for this new season. Fans are hoping for a return to the show's roots, a tighter narrative, and the authentic humor that defined its early success. The success of Season 4 is not just about continuing the story; it's about proving that **Ted Lasso** can still deliver the heartfelt, engaging television its audience craves, especially as it navigates new storylines and potential farewells.

## What's Next for Richmond

**Ted Lasso** Season 4 premiered on August 5, 2026, on Apple TV, with new episodes scheduled for weekly release every Wednesday through October 7. The season's focus is on Ted leading a new women's football team, a fresh direction that promises new challenges and character dynamics. Fans will be watching closely to see how this new chapter unfolds and if it can reignite the spark that made the series a critical and commercial darling. The coming weeks will reveal whether the show has successfully course-corrected or if it continues to struggle with the narrative choices that have drawn criticism.

content_raw: Can the real Ted Lasso please stand up?  The show stopped feeling like itself in season three, although some might trace its problems back to season two , when the Apple TV comedy bit off more than it could chew in an earnest attempt to go beyond feel-good television. Ted Lasso began and blew up as a heartfelt comedy during COVID-19 lockdown; it retained that spirit in the sophomore run before gradually losing momentum with overlong episodes and a shift from thoughtful humor to meandering melodrama. By season three, those sluggish runtimes and stretched-out storylines made it nearly impossible to take the latest developments in the lives of Coach Lasso seriously. That awful CGI during Beard’s season-finale wedding in the finale was the cherry on top of a stale cake.  Over three years after it last aired, the show returns in what is meant to be a soft relaunch, with Ted training a new women’s football team. All the season four trailers and cast interviews have already laid this premise out. So it’s frustrating that the show—having apparently not learned a thing during its lengthy hiatus—returns with a 42-minute outing that spins its wheels to get to the point. I understand that series co-creators Jason Sudeikis, Brendan Hunt, Joe Keely (who wrote “Home”), and new showrunner Jack Burditt want to establish why Ted chooses to return to London with his family, considering he left to be with his son in Kansas two years ago. It’s necessary to show that for Ted, Richmond is, well, home.  However, in an effort to depict this obvious fact, the series premiere relies on similarly frustrating narratives, like the protagonists’ caricaturish turns (sorry to Ms. Keeley Jones!) or relevant developments taking place offscreen. If Ted’s son and ex-wife have seemingly agreed to join Ted in London this time around, isn’t that the conversation we should be seeing to understand their current dynamic better, instead of this major turn occurring at the end of the episode via text messages? “Home” takes other avoidable detours, too, like Rebecca and Keeley’s shopping trip or Higgins at the museum, but I’m getting ahead of myself.  The episode opens with Ted as an assistant manager at a grocery store, using his overtly positive methods to teach an employee that Stealing Is Bad. His relationship with Michelle isn’t exactly romantic again, but they’re on quite friendly terms, laughing over how Henry’s principal can’t distinguish 38-year-old Public Enemy lyrics from the poetry of a troubled kid in the 2020s. What is clear is that Michelle and Ted don’t love their respective jobs, and that Henry—about to graduate in a matter of days—is also unhappy (as suggested by his messy room and sullen attitude).
